Understand how it works, down to the binary level.** [![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/rea-agents?style=flat-square&color=cb3837)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/rea-agents) [![MCP tool catalog](https://img.shields.io/badge/MCP-tool_catalog-5c4ee5?style=flat-square)](docs/mcp-contracts.md#generated-catalog) [![Node.js requirements](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-requirements-339933?style=flat-square&logo=nodedotjs&logoColor=white)](#what-you-can-analyze) [![skills.sh](https://skills.sh/b/morluto/rea?style=flat-square)](https://skills.sh/morluto/rea/reverse-engineer-anything) [![MIT license](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-f4c430?style=flat-square)](LICENSE) [![Discord](https://img.shields.io/discord/1556595354999332884?logo=discord&logoColor=white&label=Discord&color=5865F2)](https://discord.gg/GkcryMnJDM) **[Website](https://rea.tools/) · [Guides](https://rea.tools/guides/) · [Showcases](https://rea.tools/showcase/)** [Quick start](#quick-start) · [How REA works](#how-rea-works) · [What you can analyze](#what-you-can-analyze) · [Showcases](#showcases) · [Build RL environments](#build-rl-environments) · [FAQ](#faq) · [Documentation](#documentation) npx rea-agents setup
> [!IMPORTANT] > Get REA from [morluto/rea](https://github.com/morluto/rea), > [rea.tools](https://rea.tools/), or the [rea-agents npm package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/rea-agents). > Follow the installation and release links from these official sources. A similar > repository name or copied README does not establish that a download is official.




Join the Reverse Engineering Community
Discord · Q&A · Show and Tell

--- See a feature in an app that you want in your own product? Ask your agent to investigate it with REA. It can inspect the app without its source code, explain how the feature works, show the evidence, and build a version for your project. REA connects your agent to tools for inspecting native binaries, JavaScript and Electron apps, .NET assemblies, and websites. You can also use the same tools from your terminal. Analysis runs locally, and results include the evidence and limitations behind each conclusion. Setup registers REA with your agent and installs matching workflow instructions. Native analysis can use an existing Hopper, Ghidra, or IDA installation; setup can optionally install Hopper with approval. Static JavaScript analysis needs no native analysis engine. > **[Visit the REA website](https://rea.tools/)** for setup instructions, illustrated guides, and real case studies. ## Quick start On Linux, Ghidra, JADX, firmware tool launches and static JavaScript/Electron analysis require a procps-compatible `ps` on REA's `PATH` for process ownership checks. Recovery steps are in `docs/installation.md` under "Linux owned-process prerequisite". ### Set up your agent With Node.js and npm installed, run: ```bash npx rea-agents setup ``` Choose your agents, review the proposed changes, and approve them. Setup adds REA's MCP server and matching workflow instructions, with backups of existing configuration. Restart your agent afterward. Setup supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build and [other agents](docs/installation.md#supported-agents). See [installation and setup](docs/installation.md) for provider configuration and manual MCP registration. MCP uses compact input schemas by default to reduce context overhead. Set `REA_MCP_INPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE=full` in your MCP registration when you need the complete advertised field guidance and nested validation details. Both profiles keep the full tool set and canonical server validation. See "Compact input schema profile" in the MCP contracts guide. Complete output schemas are advertised by default. If your client caps the complete `tools/list` frame, set `REA_MCP_OUTPUT_SCHEMA_PROFILE=compact` to bound each advertised output schema, or `off` to omit output schemas entirely. Both settings keep canonical server-side validation and complete structured results. See "Output schemas" in the MCP contracts guide. ### Ask your agent ```text Understand how search works in the Notes app, show me the evidence, and build a similar feature for my project. ``` Replace Notes with your target app and the feature you want to understand. ### Use the terminal Inspect an extracted JavaScript/Electron app directory or ASAR: ```bash npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json ``` The result includes modules, imports, Electron boundaries and their evidence. Replace the path with your target, such as `"D:/apps/example"` on Windows. To install the `rea` command for regular use: ```bash npm install --global rea-agents rea --help ``` For native analysis, configure a provider first. See the [CLI and Evidence guide](docs/cli.md) for native commands, provider selection, snapshots and scripting. ### Update REA REA changes quickly, and new releases include frequent bug fixes. Keep your installation up to date. For a CLI installed with `npm install --global` or `bun add --global`: ```bash rea update ``` `rea --update` is an alias for this verified workflow and accepts the same global output flags. Use `rea update` when combining it with other command controls. Updater commands retain at most 4 MiB of stdout and stderr combined. Oversized metadata replies are rejected after the command exits; verbose installs continue with bounded diagnostics. Human progress output respects terminal backpressure and waits for submitted writes to finish. Bun global updates require Bun 1.2.17 or later. With an older Bun release, upgrade Bun manually before running `rea update`. To refresh your agent registrations and skill, run the setup command printed by the update. If you use `npx`, update your agent setup with: ```bash npx rea-agents@latest setup ``` Review the setup changes and restart your agent. For one-off CLI commands, use `npx rea-agents@latest` followed by the command. With Bun, use `bunx rea-agents@latest` in place of `npx rea-agents@latest`. ## How REA works Your agent calls REA through MCP to inspect the target and trace relevant code. REA returns findings with their evidence. The agent uses them to ask follow-up questions, explain the behavior, or write and test an implementation. CLI commands use the same workflows. ![REA investigation flow: your agent asks about a local target, REA inspects and traces it using analysis tools, and the agent uses the returned code, references and unknowns to explain, implement and test.](website/public/assets/figures/rea-investigation-flow.svg) [Open the full-size figure](website/public/assets/figures/rea-investigation-flow.svg). ## What you can analyze REA requires Node.js 22.x (>=22.23.4), 24.x (>=24.22.1), or 26.12.1+, plus npm. Additional tools and host support depend on the target: | Target | What REA returns | Requirements and guide | | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Desktop installations | Runtime candidates, supporting files, component markers and next probes | Built-in bounded directory/header inspection; [desktop applications](docs/desktop-applications.md) | | Native binaries | Pseudocode, assembly, strings, symbols, calls and references | Hopper, Ghidra or IDA; [native analysis](docs/native-investigation.md) | | Offline ELF layout | Sections, segments, original symbols/relocations and static mitigation candidates | Caller-supplied pwntools on Linux x64; [binary diagnostics](docs/binary-diagnostics.md) | | Go binaries | Embedded compiler version, modules, replacements and build settings | Built-in static ELF/PE/thin Mach-O inspection; no Go installation required | | GPU code objects | CUDA/HIP targets, selected kernel parameters and resources, retained PTX text | Built-in static ELF/PE/fatbin/CUBIN/PTX inspection; [GPU code objects](docs/gpu-code-objects.md) | | Model artifacts | GGUF / safetensors metadata, tensor declarations and derived totals | Built-in header inspection; optional full-file hash; [model files](docs/model-artifacts.md) | | IL2CPP metadata | Unity global-metadata.dat assembly images, type and method names and index ranges | Built-in static decoding of versions 24, 27, 29, 31 and 39; no Unity required | | Godot PCK | Archive inventory and extraction, original header/directory facts and selected content identities | Built-in static formats 2, 3 and 4; no Godot required | | Rust binaries | Embedded cargo-auditable crate names, versions, sources and dependency edges | Built-in static ELF/PE/thin Mach-O inspection; [Rust binaries](docs/rust-binaries.md) | | PE certificates | Authenticode WIN_CERTIFICATE entries and PKCS#7 signer/X.509 identity fields | Built-in static PE inspection; [PE certificates](docs/pe-certificates.md) | | PE imports | Import and delay-load DLL names, ordinals, IAT RVAs and pefile import hash | Built-in static PE inspection; [PE imports](docs/pe-imports.md) | | ELF notes | PT_NOTE/SHT_NOTE owners, types, GNU build-id and ABI-tag fields | Built-in static ELF inspection; [ELF notes](docs/elf-notes.md) | | Apple IPS crashes | .ips metadata, threads, images, registers and documented crash classes | Built-in static JSON inspection; [Apple IPS](docs/apple-ips.md) | | Linux kernel modules | .modinfo keys, __versions CRCs, this_module presence, and signature trailer | Built-in static ELF inspection; [kernel modules](docs/kernel-modules.md) | | Erlang BEAM | IFF chunks, atoms, exports, imports, lambdas and the Code header | Built-in static BEAM inspection; [Erlang BEAM](docs/erlang-beam.md) | | WASM artifact | Validation, sections, exact import/export WAT forms and decoded WAT | Caller-supplied WABT 1.0.42; `inspect_wasm_artifact` | | EVM bytecode | Dispatch selectors, byte offsets, inferred arguments and mutability | Local raw/hex carrier on Linux x64; [offline EVM guide](docs/evm-bytecode.md) | | SQLite databases | Tables, columns, indexes, views, triggers and selected ordinary-table rows | Local database/WAL snapshot; Node.js 24.x >=24.15 or 26+ with native SQLite limits | | Recorded Linux crashes | Raw notes, every recorded thread's registers/signals and optional mapping candidates | Caller-supplied pwntools on Linux x64; optional GDB/pwndbg; [recorded crashes](docs/recorded-crashes.md) | | JavaScript / Electron | Modules, imports, source maps, routes, IPC and native add-on relationships | Node.js and npm; Linux: procps-compatible `ps`; [application analysis](docs/javascript-application-workflows.md) | | Websites | Page structure, scripts, network observations and requested screenshots | A Chrome-family browser; [browser analysis](docs/browser-observation.md) | | Saved network captures | Requests, responses, exposed payloads and source locations | HAR or Fiddler Everywhere SAZ; mitmdump on Linux for native mitmproxy; [capture guide](docs/web-network-captures.md) | | .NET assemblies | Metadata, CIL instructions, declared native dependencies and build comparisons | None (static only); [managed-code guide](docs/managed-code-analysis.md) | | Android APKs | Manifest declarations, classes, decompiled methods and references | Headless JADX and a full JDK on Linux/macOS/Windows x64; [Android guide](docs/android-analysis.md) | | APK signatures | v1/v2/v3/v3.1 signers, certificate fingerprints, key rotation and digest self-consistency | None (static only); `inspect_apk_signature` | | Android devices | Devices, packages, processes, logs, dumps, screen captures, and APK/file transfers | Caller-supplied adb (emulator or hardware); [ADB guide](docs/adb-device-analysis.md) | | JEB projects | Engine-backed project units, artifact digests and type/method pseudo-code | A caller-started JEB client serving MCP, selected with REA_JEB_MCP_URL; [JEB guide](docs/jeb-analysis.md) | | Android resources | Decoded manifest, string tables, locales and version facts | Caller-supplied Apktool launcher; [resource guide](docs/apktool-resource-analysis.md) | | Flutter apps | Dart snapshot hash, per-ABI library digests and engine build provenance | None (static APK parsing); [Flutter guide](docs/flutter-analysis.md) | | Firmware | Regions, extraction results and native-analysis handoffs | Binwalk / Unblob on Linux; [firmware guide](docs/firmware-analysis.md) | | Recorded packets | Selected fields, repeated values, filters and decode-as rules | Linux: TShark 4.x + prlimit; [capture guide](docs/packet-captures.md) | | Packet summaries | Endpoints, DNS, TLS SNI, protocol distribution and HTTP requests | Caller-supplied tshark and capinfos (Linux-verified); [pcap guide](docs/pcap-analysis.md) | | Recorded logic signals | Decoder annotations, sample ranges and diagnostics | Linux: sigrok-cli 0.7.2 + prlimit; [signal recordings](docs/signal-recordings.md) | | Packages and resources | File inventories, digests, plists, Apple bundle anatomy and extracted resources | [Artifact and JavaScript guide](docs/javascript-artifact-reconstruction.md), [Apple applications](docs/apple-application-analysis.md) | | Process behavior | Terminal output, interactions, exit and filesystem observations, and run comparisons | Linux/macOS with a native PTY; [process capture](docs/process-capture.md) | | PyInstaller executables | CArchive members, Python version, entry scripts and extracted bytecode | None (static only); [Python packaged applications](docs/python-packaged-applications.md) | Static JavaScript and .NET inspection read the supplied files without running the application. Runtime capture runs or interacts with the selected target using your user permissions; each runtime guide describes its effects. For offline native-binary inspection, REA also supports caller-supplied GNU objdump and Rizin. See the [reverse-engineering tools guide](docs/reverse-engineering-tools.md) for provider setup, CLI commands, and Evidence limitations. REA does not install or update either provider. Native formats and host support vary by provider. See [Hopper and Ghidra setup](docs/installation.md#hopper), the [IDA guide](docs/ida-provider.md) (including an optional native MCP bridge), the [Kuna decompiler guide](docs/kuna-provider.md), and [experimental Windows Ghidra support](docs/windows-ghidra-p0.md). Ghidra also supports [16-bit DOS analysis](docs/ghidra-dos.md). For large binaries, raise the provider's startup deadline with `REA_GHIDRA_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS` or `REA_HOPPER_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS`. For provider selection, see the [CLI guide](docs/cli.md#choose-a-provider). Check [release availability](docs/installation.md#released-package-and-main) for features added since the latest npm release. ## Showcases ### DX-Ball: reconstruct a sound-pan calculation Follow a sound call into its position-to-pan helper, inspect the instructions, and turn incomplete pseudocode into C. The reconstruction passes 3,205 original-x86 cases and reproduces all 63 compiled function bytes. [Read the case study](https://rea.tools/showcase/dx-ball/) · [Reconstruction repository](https://github.com/N0zoM1z0/dx-ball) ### Notion: trace the Electron clipboard bridge Find the renderer's clipboard API, follow it through preload and IPC into the main process, and inspect the rich clipboard format. [Read the case study](https://rea.tools/showcase/notion/) ### TH04: recover a DOS bullet-ring calculation Inspect the original PC-98 game's 16-bit instructions, recover the fixed and aimed angle calculations, and compare the reconstructed C++ with the historical compiler output. [Read the case study](https://rea.tools/showcase/th04/) · [Reconstruction repository](https://github.com/N0zoM1z0/th04) ### Build RL environments with REA Record a web app session, turn its API into tools, and export an environment an AI agent can use. Run it with AgentEnv, then add tasks and reward checks for RL training or evaluation. [Read the guide](https://rea.tools/guides/rl-environments/) · [Watch the video](https://x.com/reatools/status/2112574822584918075?s=20) If you've used REA on something interesting, we'd love to see it. Share your case in an [issue](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues) or a [pull request](https://github.com/morluto/rea/pulls), including the target, your question, how REA helped, and what you found. ## Build RL environments Give an AI agent a local environment to practice tasks such as finding an issue or creating a folder, without running the original app. Use it for reinforcement learning (RL) or to test how well an agent completes tasks. REA turns recorded API requests and responses into tools the agent can call. The environment uses the recorded data and supports changes only when the recording confirms their effects. With REA set up in your agent, replace the example URL and folder tasks below with your own: ```text Use REA to build an RL environment from my test web app at http://127.0.0.1:3000. Cover listing, creating, renaming, and deleting folders. You may create and remove test folders. Leave existing data unchanged. Save it in a folder named my-env. Check which operations work and tell me how to run it. ```
Use the command line instead Use these commands if you already have a file containing the app’s recorded browser requests and responses. Running the result also requires AgentEnv and Docker. ```sh rea environment-build ./session.har ./my-env --name my-env --json agent-env run ./my-env ```
REA exports a runnable environment with a basic test to check that it starts and responds. Use it with your RL framework to define task goals, add reward checks, and run training. [Build an environment](https://rea.tools/guides/rl-environments/) · [Environment reference](docs/agent-environments.md) · [Watch the demo on X](https://x.com/reatools/status/2112574822584918075?s=20) ## FAQ
Which agents can use REA? Any agent that supports local MCP servers. Setup configures the [supported agents](docs/installation.md#supported-agents); other clients can use [manual MCP registration](docs/installation.md#mcp-registry).
Do I need Hopper, Ghidra or IDA? Deep native analysis uses one of them. Static JavaScript and .NET inspection work without a native analysis engine. Setup can install Hopper after approval; Ghidra and IDA use your existing installations. See [provider setup](docs/installation.md#hopper).
Do I need to start Hopper first? REA starts Hopper when an operation needs it. On macOS, a first-run dialog may ask you to choose demo mode or activate your license. Complete that prompt in the same user session before your first CLI/MCP operation or unattended job. Open Hopper manually if needed. See [Hopper startup and troubleshooting](docs/installation.md#launcher-paths-and-troubleshooting).
What does installing the skill from skills.sh do? The skill supplies investigation instructions for your agent. Use `npx rea-agents setup` to register REA's MCP server and install the matching instructions, then restart your agent. See [skill-only installation](docs/installation.md#skill-only-installation).
What code does REA return? Native analysis returns pseudocode and assembly. JavaScript/Electron analysis recovers modules and their relationships. Your agent uses these findings to write and test an implementation; the [showcases](#showcases) give worked examples.
Does REA upload my app? REA analyzes targets locally. Your agent receives the tool results, and its model provider has its own data policy.
What should I do if I hit a bug? Update first; a recent release may already fix it. For a CLI installed with `npm install --global` or `bun add --global`: ```bash rea update ``` For agent setup through `npx`: ```bash npx rea-agents@latest setup ``` If you're using an agent, complete the [setup refresh](#update-rea) and restart it. Retry the same task. If the problem persists, [open an issue](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues) with your REA version, target type, steps to reproduce and error output.
## Documentation Start with the website's [worked guides](https://rea.tools/guides/). For exact options, prerequisites and result contracts: - [Installation and setup](docs/installation.md): agent registration, provider configuration, updates and uninstall. - [Readiness and troubleshooting](docs/installation.md#check-readiness-for-your-task): diagnose one agent or analysis engine. - [CLI and Evidence](docs/cli.md): commands, provider selection, snapshots, import/export and exit statuses. - [MCP contracts](docs/mcp-contracts.md) and [agent prompts](docs/mcp-prompts.md): tool results, sessions and guided investigations. - [Tool catalog](docs/mcp-contracts.md#generated-catalog): generated inventory of tools, providers and CLI commands. - [Roadmap](docs/roadmap.md): planned work and capability trackers. Report vulnerabilities through [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). ## Star history 🎉 **300,000 GitHub stars — thank you!** Thanks to everyone using REA, reporting bugs, requesting features, testing builds, and contributing fixes. ## Disclaimer See [DISCLAIMER.md](DISCLAIMER.md) for responsible-use guidance. The project's position on illegal or unauthorized use covers all REA versions, distribution channels, and platforms; each copy retains its applicable licenses. REA is for lawful research, education, interoperability, software preservation, and analysis of software you own or are authorized to examine. ## Contributing We'd love your help with REA! [Open an issue](https://github.com/morluto/rea/issues) to report a bug or suggest a feature, or [send a pull request](https://github.com/morluto/rea/pulls) to improve the code or docs. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for development setup and checks, [testing](docs/testing.md) for verification lanes, and the [architecture map](docs/architecture.mermaid) for selected layers and dependency paths. ## License [MIT](LICENSE) REA-authored code is licensed under MIT. Third-party material retains its own licenses and copyright notices; see [Third-party notices](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md) for the dependency inventory, preserved license texts, and external-tool terms. **You must legally obtain and be authorized to use commercial tools**, including IDA Pro / Hex-Rays decompilers, Hopper, and JEB, under their applicable licenses. REA grants no tool license, key, or activation entitlement. Trials and demos remain subject to vendor terms, including user, feature, automation, and output sharing restrictions. Cracked copies, stolen keys, unauthorized key sharing, and bypassing license restrictions are not authorized. This guidance does not amend MIT or third-party licenses.

items.description: Debloat any Android or Google TV over Wi-Fi and get an Apple TV-style home.
items.readme_text:
**The viral tweet:** [x.com/gathint/status/2111379569030939102](https://x.com/gathint/status/2111379569030939102) On 17 October 2026 I posted a before and after of my parents' TV, cleaned up by Claude Code over Wi-Fi. It reached 7.4M views, people started doing the same to their own TVs, and their replies turned into the lists here: 170+ TV models from 200+ contributors in four days. The repo was called tv-vibehack until the 19th; old links work. **Themes, switches and add-ons:** [cleanyour.tv/addons](https://cleanyour.tv/addons) **Official links:** the website is [cleanyour.tv](https://cleanyour.tv) and the code, launcher and tools live only in this repo. Other domains using the name, such as cleanyourtv.com, are not run by this project ([#1004](https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv/issues/1004)). ## How it works Android TVs have the same debug bridge as Android phones. Switch on USB debugging in the TV's developer options, allow your computer once, and the rest is standard Android tooling: | Step | What happens | |---|---| | **Back up** | The list of installed packages and settings. | | **Disable** | The manufacturer's telemetry, ad services, content rows and preloaded junk, with `pm disable-user`. Nothing is uninstalled, so a restore script can undo every step. | | **Install** | A small native launcher, made the default home screen. | **No root, no cable, nothing uninstalled, and a one-line restore if you change your mind.** The bloat differs by brand, so the prompt has your coding assistant discover it on your TV and ask before touching anything you might use. ## Quick start | You have | Do this | |---|---| | **A computer** | Use the prompt with a coding assistant: the three steps below. | | **Only an Android phone** | Use the community-built [Clean Your TV app](https://cleanyour.tv/app) by [@udhaykumarbala](https://github.com/udhaykumarbala): connect, analyse, clean, in about five minutes. No laptop, no coding agent. | With a computer, you need it on the same Wi-Fi as the TV and a coding assistant with shell access. Any of these work: Claude Code (on [0G Private Computer](https://pc.0g.ai) or an [Anthropic plan](https://claude.com/pricing)), [Codex](https://github.com/openai/codex) or [Gemini CLI](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli). | Where | What to do | |---|---| | **1. On the TV** | Settings → Device Preferences → About → press OK on **Build** seven times → back → Developer options → **USB debugging** on. If you see a Network or ADB debugging toggle, turn that on too. Keep the TV on. | | **2. On your computer** | Clone the repo and open that folder in your assistant (`git clone https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv`), then paste [`PROMPT.md`](PROMPT.md) and fill in your TV model. | | **3. Follow along** | Accept "Allow USB debugging?" on the TV, then answer the checklist: which apps you use, the dock size and app order, whether to keep the voice assistant, Chromecast and updates. | Cloning matters: the assistant reuses this repo's `tools/disable.sh` and `launcher/build-and-install.sh` instead of writing its own, and that is where the backup, the Home guard and the restore record live. The assistant backs up, debloats, builds and installs the launcher, and checks each step with screenshots pulled from the TV. With this repo as context it takes about fifteen minutes. ## What you get A home screen that looks like an Apple TV and gets out of the way: | Part | What it looks like | |---|---| | **A pitch-black home** | A dock of your four favourite apps in a rounded band, where Apple TV puts it. | | **A top shelf** | Names the focused app in large type, with an ambient glow in a colour taken from its artwork. | | **The rest of your apps in a grid** | Slides up when you press Down. | | **One floating glass highlight** | Springs from tile to tile. The focused tile lifts and shows its name. | | **Three frosted buttons** | Inputs (HDMI ports under the names you gave them in the TV's settings, AV, Live TV), Wi-Fi or Ethernet with the network name, Settings. | | **A greeting, a thin clock and the date** | In [Outfit](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Outfit), and a matching Clock screensaver. The tools need Python 3 and nothing else. `tools/tv.py` talks to network ADB on port 5555. Windows (PowerShell) Every script has a PowerShell twin next to it. On Windows with Android Studio installed nothing else is needed: ```powershell python -m venv tools\venv; tools\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r tools\requirements.txt powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File launcher\build-and-install.ps1 -TvHost 192.168.1.50 powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File tools\disable.ps1 -TvHost 192.168.1.50 examples\xiaomi-mi-tv-4a\debloat.txt ```
How the scripts protect Home The install scripts ask the TV which launcher owns Home and only disable one they recognise, the four in `KNOWN_STOCK_LAUNCHERS`: `com.google.android.tvlauncher`, `com.google.android.apps.tv.launcherx`, `com.google.android.leanbacklauncher` and Xiaomi's `com.mitv.tvhome` (PatchWall). Pass `STOCK_LAUNCHER=` (`-StockLauncher`) to override, or `none` to leave it alone. `tools/disable.sh` (`disable.ps1`) applies the same rule before it disables anything: if the list contains the app that owns Home and no other app on the TV answers HOME, it skips that entry, says why, and disables the rest of the list. The setup wizard, the settings apps, a vendor `FallbackHome` and factory-test apps (Xiaomi's `com.duokan.factorytest`) answer HOME too and don't count. So a list applied before the launcher handover cannot leave the TV with nothing to start. Run the same list again once `launcher/build-and-install.sh` has made the new launcher Home and the entry is applied; `FORCE_HOME=1` (`$env:FORCE_HOME`) disables it anyway.
Where your lists can live Debloat list paths passed to `disable.sh` and `restore.sh` are relative to the directory you run from, so your own lists can live outside the repository. Absolute paths also work.
## The microphone, and what can be said about it "Which of these packages is listening?" has no honest one-line answer, and a permission scan makes it worse: on many sets most packages run as `android.uid.system`, so fifty of them show `RECORD_AUDIO: granted=true` and none of them record anything. On others the microphone is in the remote, not the panel, and a package with no audio permission at all still sees everything on screen — ACR clients such as `tv.inscape.tvclient.inscapeacr` identify content from the picture and need only `INTERNET`. `tools/privacy.py` reports what the TV actually says instead of guessing: `TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/privacy.py` prints voice, ACR and telemetry candidates in three groups, each with its evidence — named by the firmware's own `voice_interaction_service`, a known component from [`examples/`](examples/), or nothing but a matching name — plus whether the package declares `RECORD_AUDIO`, whether it shares the system UID, and whether the returned AppOps history contains microphone access. A configured mode or a rejected attempt alone is not evidence of access. `--write privacy.txt` turns the identified candidates into a normal debloat list, so applying it and undoing it are the commands you already use (`tools/disable.sh`, `tools/restore.sh`). Packages that only matched by name stay out unless you pass `--include-low`; they are the ones to check with `dumpsys package ` first. What the audit cannot do is prove intent. `appops` shows an op was touched, not what happened to the stream afterwards, and no scan of package names proves a TV is or is not recording. Disabling an assistant is a trade you make with a specific loss (the remote's mic button, voice search inside apps), which is why the report names that loss per package instead of calling it a win. ## The launcher A small native home screen for Android TV: **about 523 KB**, plain Java, built for TVs with 1 GB of RAM. No blur, no video, no network permission, no background services. The **TV** needs Android 8.0 (API 26) or newer: `minSdk` is a compile-time floor in [`launcher/app/build.gradle`](launcher/app/build.gradle), and the install script asks the TV for `ro.build.version.sdk` before it builds, so an older set is told both numbers instead of failing at `pm install` (see [Troubleshooting](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md) for what is left on such a set). | What | How it works | |---|---| | **Configure** | Dock order, hidden apps, Live TV app, 4 to 7 tiles per row, reduced motion. All in [`config.xml`](launcher/app/src/main/res/values/config.xml) | | **Settings on the TV** | Hold OK on Settings for launcher settings. Optional `launcher_settings_button` makes a normal click open them directly; TV settings remain on the settings page and their app tile. | | **Themes** | Background, wallpaper and layout from a `config.json` pushed over Wi-Fi, no rebuild. ten ship in [`themes/`](themes/), the built-in `default/` included | | **28 languages** | Follows the TV's language, with a fully mirrored right-to-left layout for Hebrew | | **App library** | Optional: browse every installed app and add or remove Home shortcuts. Build it yourself It needs JDK 17 and Android SDK platform 34. On macOS: `brew install openjdk@17 android-commandlinetools` and `sdkmanager "platforms;android-34" "build-tools;34.0.0"`. On Linux the install script finds `~/Android/Sdk` and the `java` on your PATH.
Configure [`config.xml`](launcher/app/src/main/res/values/config.xml) sets the dock order, hidden apps, the Live TV package, columns (tiles shrink from 5 up), rows under the dock, an optional VPN app for the network pill, and `reduced_motion` for TVs whose GPU cannot keep up. Themes set the same keys plus a background colour and a wallpaper.
Launcher settings and the default home - Click **Settings** for the TV's own settings. Hold OK on it for its menu: **Launcher settings** (with `launcher_settings_button` a click opens those instead and the menu leaves the row out), **Native settings** where the TV ships a settings app of its own beside Android's - Xiaomi China, TCL/FFALCON and Fire OS are in `settings_fallback_components` - because that app holds pages Android's has no row for, such as Xiaomi's Account & Security with the ADB switch; **Module cards** with `module_cards`; **Edit dock** with `dock_row`; **Reorder apps**; and **Restart…** while `HomeKeyService` runs, which opens the system power menu (a launcher may not restart the TV itself). The launcher's own page has these rows, top to bottom: - **Reorder apps**, only with `launcher_settings_button`: OK picks an app up, the arrows move it, Back places it, and Back again finishes. - **Apps per row** 4, 5, 6 or 7; **Rows below dock** 0 to 3, how many rows of tiles stay visible under the dock band; **Dock band opacity** 100%, 70%, 50% or 30%. The last two only do anything while the dock is its own row (`dock_row`, on by default). - **Wallpaper**: one picture from the theme's collection (or its `wallpaper.jpg`), **None**, or **Theme default**. A pick holds that picture and stops the rotation until you choose Theme default, press Follow theme, or push the theme again. - **Animations** on or off, and **Advanced effects** (tile lift, icon zoom and smooth ambient-colour transitions; they may use more memory) once animations are on. - **Open on start**, only with `open_on_start_choice`: Off, or an app that opens instead of Home the first time Home comes up after the TV starts. Once per boot, so Home and Back still reach the launcher. - **Follow theme (reset on-TV choices)**, which clears every choice above. Pushing or resetting a theme clears them too. - **Choose default home** opens Android's home picker, and **TV system settings** the TV's own settings page. - **Change the default home:** Launcher settings and the optional Default-home tile (`show_home_settings_shortcut`) open Android's home picker. Choose the original launcher to stop using CleanYourTV as Home, or CleanYourTV to return. The original launcher must be enabled; if the install script disabled it, run the restore script below first. Some TVs provide no home picker.
Languages English, German, Danish, Spanish, Catalan, French, Russian, Serbian (Latin), Polish, Czech, Italian, Portuguese, Turkish, Arabic, Hebrew, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese (Taiwan), Thai, Finnish, Vietnamese, Bangla, Indonesian, Norwegian Bokmål, Dutch, Uzbek (Latin), Ukrainian and Korean. The launcher follows the TV's language. Android 13+ can set it for the launcher alone: `tools/tv.py 'cmd locale set-app-locales com.gathin.tvhome --locales ca'`. Hebrew mirrors the layout: menu buttons on the left, date and clock on the right with the greeting above, dock and app rows starting on the right with matching remote navigation, the input selector's icons and labels on the right, and dates with the month prefix ב (for example, 19 באוקטובר). The Clock screensaver right-aligns its date and time. Russian covers every screen, including race weekends, festival greetings and the Shamsi date. Other languages keep their original layouts.
Module cards Any TV app can declare its own tile (label, caption, glow). The launcher asks you once per app, keeps it hidden by default, and remembers the answer for that app's signing key and card name. Hold OK on Settings and choose Module cards to change your mind. How to make one: [`docs/modules.md`](docs/modules.md); the contract: [`docs/specs/card.md`](docs/specs/card.md).
Clock screensaver Pick "Clock" in the TV's screensaver settings, or over ADB: ```bash tools/tv.py 'settings put secure screensaver_components com.gathin.tvhome/.ClockDream; settings put secure screensaver_enabled 1' ```
Remote keys - An optional accessibility service keeps the remote's **Input** button working on Google TV (`INPUT_KEY_SERVICE=1` at install). - It can bring back other buttons only the stock launcher answered, such as the **YouTube** button (`app_keys` and `input_key_keycodes`, in config.xml or a theme; `HOME_KEY_SERVICE=1` reads `app_keys` too). - A `hold:` prefix on an `app_keys` entry gives that button a second app: a normal press opens the unprefixed app, holding for half a second opens the hold one (by keycode or `hold:scan:...`). An entry can name an activity (`package/.Activity`), such as an add-on's quick bar, instead of the app's launcher entry. - In place of an app, an `app_keys` entry can name an action: `back`, `home`, `recents`, `mute`, `sleep`, `screensaver`, `settings` or `wifi`, so a spare colour button can mute the TV or, held, put it in standby. - `HOME_KEY_SERVICE=1` also fixes sticks whose Home key sends ALL_APPS, and opens Settings from the remote's **gear** button, even one Android does not map (scancodes or keycodes in config.xml). - With `settings_key_panel` the gear opens a [small quick settings panel](docs/quick-settings-panel.jpg) over Home or any app: TV settings, Display, Network, Apps and Launcher settings.
Navigation and artwork Up and Down move one row. The top buttons never fall through to tiles, and Down from them returns to the dock tile you came from. The last focused app is remembered, and installing or removing an app refreshes the tiles while Home is open. App banners load at xhdpi or better, so low-density TV UIs do not downsample them before the focus zoom.
## Restoring your TV Keep the list you applied. One line puts the TV back the way it was: ```bash TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/restore.sh examples//debloat.txt # Android TV TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/restore.sh examples//debloat.txt com.google.android.apps.tv.launcherx # Google TV ``` | What | How | |---|---| | **A record comes first** | Before `tools/disable.sh` changes anything it writes down what the TV looked like, in `~/.cleanyourtv/`. | | **Restore replays it** | A package you had disabled yourself stays disabled, and Home goes back to the component that owned it. | | **The launcher stays installed** | Remove it from the TV's Settings → Apps if you want it gone. | | **No computer?** | If the TV is unreachable, its own Settings → Apps page can re-enable packages too. |
What the record holds, and what happens without one Before `tools/disable.sh` changes anything it writes down what the TV looked like: for every package in the list whether it was enabled, already disabled or not installed, which component owned Home, and the three animation scales. That record lives in `~/.cleanyourtv/`, one file per TV and list, and a second run of the same list keeps the first record instead of saving the cleaned-up state over it. If you added packages to the list since, that run adds them to the record before disabling them, and a listed package that was not installed then but is installed and enabled now is recorded as enabled. `check.py --fix` does the same before it disables anything. Keep the list you applied. The restore script replays the record, so a package you had disabled yourself stays disabled and Home goes back to the component that owned it: The `stock launcher` argument is only a fallback: with a record, the launcher that actually owned Home is the one that gets it back, and the argument is used only when nothing answered HOME at the time or this project's launcher owned it. The stock launcher is enabled again either way, unless it was already disabled when the record was taken. Without a record (an older run, or a record you deleted) the script says so and falls back to enabling the whole list and resetting the scales to `1.0`, which is what it used to do. It leaves the new launcher installed (remove it from the TV's Settings → Apps if you want it gone) and does not know about packages you disabled outside the list. To switch back later, run the install script again; it works out which launcher to disable even when Home has fallen back to Android's chooser. If the TV is unreachable, its own Settings → Apps page can re-enable packages too.
## After a firmware update An update installs over the cleaned-up system: the listed packages come back, Home goes to the stock launcher, and new preloads appear that no list mentions. Nothing else here notices, so compare the TV with the list you applied. The check and `--fix` reach the TV over network ADB. If you closed ADB as [Isn't ADB access a security hole?](#questions-people-ask) describes, open it again first: USB debugging, and Network/ADB debugging if the TV has it, back on as in [Quick start](#quick-start) step 1. On a TV whose port 5555 only opens through Wireless debugging, switch that on as well, pair it again with the stock `adb` and run `adb tcpip 5555`, as in [Doing it by hand](#doing-it-by-hand). Closing revoked this computer's authorisation, so accept "Allow USB debugging?" on the TV when the check connects. While ADB is closed the check can only report "could not reach the TV", even with the TV on and `TV_HOST` right. Close ADB the same way once you are done. With it open: ```bash TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/check.py examples//debloat.txt ``` It exits with `0` when the TV still matches the list, `1` when something drifted, and `2` when it could not check at all: the TV did not answer, nobody accepted the "Allow USB debugging?" prompt in time, the list path is not there, the list disables Android's core packages, or, under `--fix`, the recovery record for this TV and list cannot be read or updated (nothing is changed on the TV then). Only 1 is drift, so a job that mails on 1 alone stays quiet while the check never ran; mail on anything but 0, or on 2 as well, and a weekly job on a home server or a Pi is enough to hear about it: ```bash 0 9 * * 1 cd ~/cleanyourtv && TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/check.py examples//debloat.txt ``` `TV_HOST` is read before any of that: a run that leaves it unset stops in `tools/tv.py` with its own message and also exits 1, so set it in the job line, as above, where cron does not inherit it from your shell. The job only gets an answer from a TV that keeps network ADB listening between runs and has accepted "Allow USB debugging?" for the computer that runs it with "Always allow from this computer" ticked: without the tick the TV asks again at every run, and with nobody there to accept, the run exits 2. A port left listening is the one [Isn't ADB access a security hole?](#questions-people-ask) says to close, since anything on the network can reach it. With ADB closed as described there, every run exits 2: run the check by hand after an update instead, with ADB opened again as above. `--fix` reapplies the list to what drifted: it switches Home to the launcher the list does not disable (pass a package as the second argument if you run a fork), then disables the listed packages that came back, and reads the TV back to confirm both. It never writes a recovery record of its own, because only the first run's record holds the state from before cleanup. When there is one, `--fix` first adds to it what a second `tools/disable.sh` run would (names the list gained, and a package that was not installed then and is installed and enabled now), so `tools/restore.sh` still returns the TV to stock afterwards. Home is fixed first; if no launcher is left to take it, `--fix` changes nothing and says so. It runs the same safety checks as `tools/disable.sh` before it disables anything, since an update is the moment they matter again: it leaves setupwraith on while the saved Wi-Fi network belongs to it (`FORCE_SETUPWRAITH=1` on Ethernet), leaves the packages under the HDMI/AV inputs on (`TVINPUT_ALLOW=1` if you really want them off), leaves on the apps the TV opens its inputs and Settings with (`HANDLERS_ALLOW=1`), and never takes Home to a vendor `FallbackHome` or a factory-test app. Each package it leaves on comes with the reason and exits 1, because the TV is not back to the list until you deal with that one by hand. With `stock_home_redirect` the stock launcher can stay Home on purpose: the list leaves it out, the install script ran with `STOCK_LAUNCHER=none`, Android keeps it as Home, and `HomeKeyService` sends its home screen on to this launcher. On the Chromecast with Google TV 4K that setup matches the folder's `debloat-keep-cast.txt`, not its `debloat.txt`, which disables setupwraith and the screensaver pair the redirect setup keeps. On the Acer AR55AR2851UDPRO it is the folder's `debloat.txt`. Check those lists with the stock launcher as the second argument. Without it the check expects `com.gathin.tvhome` on Home, so every run reports Home as drift, and `--fix` tries to move Home to it, which those TVs do not keep: ```bash TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/check.py examples/google-chromecast-gtv-4k/debloat-keep-cast.txt com.google.android.apps.tv.launcherx TV_HOST=192.168.1.50 tools/venv/bin/python -I tools/check.py examples/acer-ar55ar2851udpro/debloat.txt com.google.android.tvlauncher ``` Leave the argument out where the stock launcher is meant to be off, disabled by the list or by the install script: the Chromecast's `debloat.txt`, where the install script disables launcherx, and the XGIMI projectors, where the redirect only covers for firmware that turns it back on. There the stock launcher on Home is drift, and naming it as the second argument would hide that drift. Lists that also disable the updater get no updates at all. To install one, re-enable the updater on the TV, let it update, run `check.py --fix`, and disable the updater again. On Windows the same command is `tools\venv\Scripts\python.exe -I tools\check.py `. ## When something goes wrong The full list of things that bit us is in [docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md). The three that matter most: - 🍎 **macOS blocks `adb connect`** ("No route to host") under Local Network privacy. `tools/tv.py` avoids the binary. - ⚠️ **Disable the stock launcher only after the new one is installed and running**, or Home lands on a factory test app. The install script orders this for you. - 🔁 **On Google TV the setup wizard** (`com.google.android.tungsten.setupwraith`) can take Home and crash-loop the system after the stock launcher is disabled. Disable it too, and list it in your `debloat.txt` so restore brings it back. But check `dumpsys wifi | grep -o 'cname=[^ ]*'` first: if the Wi-Fi network was saved during setup it belongs to setupwraith, and disabling it deletes the network (re-join it in Settings first; `tools/disable.sh` skips setupwraith until you do). On Google's own Chromecast and on the Google TV Streamer it also costs phone casting, see [Troubleshooting](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md). Stuck already? `tools/tv.py 'pm enable --user 0 com.google.android.apps.tv.launcherx'`. ## Questions people ask
I don't code and don't have a laptop. Can I still do this? Yes. [@udhaykumarbala](https://github.com/udhaykumarbala) built a free, open-source [phone app](https://cleanyour.tv/app) for Android that does the same cleanup over Wi-Fi: it connects to the TV, shows a plan first, saves a restore point, and only switches apps off, so everything can be put back. It's community-built.
Is this safe? Can it brick the TV? Nothing is flashed, rooted or deleted; packages are disabled in the user profile. The risk is disabling something the TV leans on, which is why lists are applied in small batches with a restore script ready. The TV's own Settings → Apps page can re-enable packages even without the tools. If the TV no longer starts far enough for that, or for ADB, a factory reset from its recovery menu is usually the way back ([#1578](https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv/issues/1578)): everything these tools change lives in the user data the reset wipes, so every disabled app comes back and the new launcher is gone, along with your own apps and accounts. A TV that still restarts in a loop after the reset points to the hardware rather than the debloat ([#1592](https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv/issues/1592)); [Troubleshooting](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md#working-on-the-tv) has the cases seen so far.
What about firmware updates? The updater is left on in most lists, so firmware updates arrive as usual. Some lists disable the TV's own updater, and on those a firmware update arrives only when you re-enable it. When one does land it installs over the cleaned-up system, so a package comes back and you re-run the script: see [After a firmware update](#after-a-firmware-update).
Won't the apps break? Streaming apps still update through the Play Store, which is left alone. The launcher just lists what is installed and launches it with intents that have been stable for a decade.
Can I do this for someone in another home? Yes, over a private [Tailscale](https://tailscale.com) link instead of the same Wi-Fi: either Tailscale on their TV, shared with you, or a computer or Apple TV at their home routing to it. Never by opening the ADB port on their router. Step by step in [docs/REMOTE.md](docs/REMOTE.md).
Isn't ADB access a security hole? It is one explicit "allow this computer" tap on the TV, the same as developing an Android app. Network ADB is plaintext on port 5555, and on firmware with `ro.adb.secure=0` any device on the LAN gets a shell, so close it when you are done: 1. On the TV: Developer options → turn **USB debugging**, **Network/ADB debugging** and **Wireless debugging** off, whichever the TV has, and revoke the USB debugging authorisations. Wireless debugging listens on a port of its own and stays open when USB debugging goes off (seen on a Chromecast with Google TV 4K). Note that port before you switch it off (`adb mdns services` lists it as `_adb-tls-connect._tcp`) and check it straight after, before the reboot: `python3 tools/adb-closed.py ` must say that port is closed. After the reboot the old number reads closed either way: Wireless debugging takes a new port each time it starts. 2. Reboot the TV, then confirm the port is gone from your computer: `python3 tools/adb-closed.py ` must say the port is closed. Wireless debugging must still be off in Developer options, and `adb mdns services` must list no `_adb-tls-connect._tcp` entry for the TV; if it came back, switch it off and check its new port as in step 1. With `nc -vz 5555`, only "Connection refused" counts: on macOS, Local Network privacy can block `nc` and make it fail with "No route to host" even while the port is open. The launcher keeps working without debugging.
Can it block ads inside apps too? Partly, with Android's Private DNS (Android 9 and newer). Point it at an ad-blocking resolver such as [AdGuard DNS](https://adguard-dns.io) and every app's ad and tracker domains stop resolving, system-wide, surviving reboots. The trade-off: that resolver then sees every DNS query the TV makes. ```bash tools/tv.py 'settings put global private_dns_specifier dns.adguard-dns.com' tools/tv.py 'settings put global private_dns_mode hostname' ``` It does not remove YouTube ads, which come from the same servers as the videos. When the TV reports "No internet", the resolver is down or unreachable and switching back restores everything: `tools/tv.py 'settings put global private_dns_mode opportunistic'`. That line needs debugging back on, because Android TV's Settings app has no Private DNS page (not in AOSP, and not in Google TV 14 on a Chromecast with Google TV 4K); ADB goes to the TV's address, so it connects while the resolver is down. A resolver that answers can still break one app on its own, so if a single app fails while the rest play, see [one app refuses to play](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md#one-app-refuses-to-play-while-the-rest-of-the-tv-is-online) before you debug the app.
Are there switches in the TV's own Settings worth flipping too? A few. They need no ADB, the remote switches them back, and the debloat leaves them in place (Usage & diagnostics and Apps only mode aside): their pages belong to Settings and Play services, which every list keeps. The paths are Google TV's; other Android TV builds move some of them. - **Settings → Privacy → Ads**: delete the advertising ID, or turn on Opt out of Ads Personalization. On Android TV it is under About → Legal information → Ads (in Device Preferences on some sets). - **Settings → Privacy → Location** off. The launcher's network pill may then say "Wi-Fi" instead of the network's name. - **Settings → Privacy → Usage & diagnostics** off, before the debloat. On a Chromecast with Google TV 4K the page comes from setupwraith, which most Google TV lists disable for the launcher swap, and on a [Hisense 50A6H4](examples/hisense-smarttv-4k-ffm-android11/debloat.txt) it opened nothing after the debloat. - **Settings → Network & Internet → Scanning always available** off. It lets Google's location service and other apps scan for Wi-Fi networks even while Wi-Fi is off, so it matters most on a TV on Ethernet. - **Settings → Accounts & Sign In → your profile → Apps only mode**, where launcherx stays enabled (`stock_home_redirect`, or the Chromecast's `debloat-keep-cast.txt`). Google TV's own home then drops its personalised recommendations and casting still works, but Search and the Assistant switch off. The switch lives in launcherx, so a list that disables launcherx takes it away. On Fire OS: Settings → Preferences → Privacy Settings, with Interest-based Ads, Device Usage Data and Collect App Usage Data off. They sync with the Amazon account, so change them in the menu, not with `settings put`.
AirPlay? Not from this repo. Chromecast built-in stays for Android phones. For iPhones, [jqssun/android-airplay-server](https://github.com/jqssun/android-airplay-server) works; an install script for it is in [PR #84](https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv/pull/84).
Can I just download the APK? Build it with the one-line script; it takes a minute and you control what goes on your TV. No prebuilt binaries.
## Contributing The most useful contribution is your TV's debloat list, so the next person with that model does not have to rediscover it. [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) has the format and the testing we ask for. Contributing through a coding agent? [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) gives it the same rules. | How to help | What it means | |---|---| | **Your TV's debloat list** | The most useful one: the next person with that model skips the discovery. | | **Launcher and prompt** | Launcher improvements and sharper prompt wording are welcome too. | | **Built something on top?** | A launcher, a port, a theme: add it to [SHOWCASE.md](SHOWCASE.md), where a hundred and twenty-one projects already live, sorted into home screens, forks, add-ons, tools and other platforms, with an index by TV brand. | The people whose work is in this repo:
Star history
## Contact | For | Where | |---|---| | **Questions about your TV** | [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv/discussions) | | **Press and queries** | [hello@itsgathin.com](mailto:hello@itsgathin.com) | | **Security issues** | Report them privately through the [Security tab](https://github.com/Gathin23/cleanyourtv/security), see [`SECURITY.md`](SECURITY.md) | ## Legal - CleanYourTV is an independent open-source project. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by any TV maker or platform. Brand and model names are used only to say which TV a list was tested on, and remain the trademarks of their owners. - It works only through settings the TV itself offers to its owner: Developer options, ADB debugging and Android's own `pm disable-user`, the same switch as Settings > Apps > Disable. It does not root the TV, flash firmware, or bypass any lock, DRM or copy protection, and the repo contains no manufacturer software, firmware or APKs. - Nothing is uninstalled, and `tools/restore.sh` puts everything back. You run it on a TV you own, at your own risk, and changing a TV's software may affect its warranty or support. - Everything here is provided as is, without warranty of any kind, under the MIT licence below. ## Licence MIT, see [`LICENSE`](LICENSE). # AI Design Skills A growing collection of design skills for AI coding tools — Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Windsurf, and anything else that reads a markdown rules file. Each skill is a self-contained folder. Install the ones you need. --- ## Skills | Skill | What it does | |---|---| | [`landing-page-design`](./skills/landing-page-design/SKILL.md) | Builds a landing page from scratch — intake questions, page structure, conversion copy, plus a full visual system (type, spacing, radius, motion) | | [`design-to-motion`](./skills/design-to-motion/SKILL.md) | Turns a static design into a pixel exact animated showcase — empty state to loaded, every visual acting out its story on a loop, background kept untouched, exported as an MP4 for X plus website and 800×500 GIFs | More on the way. [Upgrading an existing site instead of building new?](https://github.com/elayadesign/redesign-skill) That one lives in its own repo since it predates this collection. --- ## Install Pick a skill from the table above, then swap `` below for its folder name.
Claude Code ```bash mkdir -p .claude/skills git clone https://github.com/elayadesign/ai-design-skills.git /tmp/ai-design-skills cp -r /tmp/ai-design-skills/skills/ .claude/skills/ ``` Then just ask, in plain language, for what that skill covers.
Cursor ```bash mkdir -p .cursor/rules curl -o .cursor/rules/.md \ https://raw.githubusercontent.com/elayadesign/ai-design-skills/main/skills//SKILL.md ``` Or paste the file into **Settings → Rules for AI**.
Codex / Windsurf / other Copy the skill's `SKILL.md` into whatever your tool uses for project rules: | Tool | Path | |---|---| | Codex | `AGENTS.md` | | Windsurf | `.windsurfrules` | | Cline | `.clinerules` | | Generic | paste into your system prompt |
Claude.ai (no terminal) Download the skill's `SKILL.md` and upload it to a Project, or attach it to a chat and say *"follow this."*
--- ## Make it yours Every skill's design values (fonts, colors, spacing, motion) live in one section near the bottom of its file. Fork this repo, edit that section, and the rest of the skill follows automatically. --- ## Credits `landing-page-design` adapts content realism and motion ideas from [Leonxlnx/taste-skill](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill) by Leon Lin, MIT licensed. Details are at the end of [its SKILL.md](./skills/landing-page-design/SKILL.md#credits). `design-to-motion` adapts a few general motion rules from [emilkowalski/skills](https://github.com/emilkowalski/skills), [Owl-Listener/designer-skills](https://github.com/Owl-Listener/designer-skills), and [dylantarre/animation-principles](https://github.com/dylantarre/animation-principles), all MIT licensed. Details are at the end of [its SKILL.md](./skills/design-to-motion/SKILL.md#credits). --- ## License MIT. Use it, fork it, ship it, sell what you build with it. No attribution needed.

/ jitterRatio。将这三项嵌套在 backoff:{} 中， 调度器读到 undefined，于是 undefined \* 2ⁿ = NaN，而持久会话日志会直接拒绝非有限数值—— 一个本可恢复的瞬时故障因此导致整轮对话报废。应返回已解析完毕的扁平策略。 **一次被中断的工具调用会永久污染该会话。** 缺少对应结果的工具调用在重放时，上游返回 400 invalid_request_error，此后该会话中的每一次请求都会失败。本插件在发送前修复配对， 三种线协议共用同一处修复逻辑。 **未在 inject 中声明的服务，属性直读会抛错（与返回 undefined 不同）；而 ctx.get() 在服务 "尚未被 provide 出来"时返回 undefined。** 这两条本轮各自触发过一次问题：将 inject 缩减为仅剩 llm 之后，typeof ctx.interval === 'function' 直接抛出 cannot get property "timer" without inject（ctx.interval 是 timer 服务上的 mixin），插件在所有 composition 中 均不再激活；改用 ctx.get('webServer') 后返回 undefined——原因不在于缺少 web server，而在于插件先于 web 半身加载——导致设置页路由全部未注册。正确做法是 ctx.inject(deps, callback)：为所需服务开启一条独立的 fiber 使其待命， 避免在加载瞬间做一次性判断。 ## 为什么按 body 的形状而不是 Content-Type 读响应 该车道会在高负载下以 200 + application/json 返回完整的 SSE 帧序列。旧实现依赖 header， 于是 await response.text() 将整条流读成字符串、JSON.parse 失败、整轮报废——而该 错误对象携带 status: 200，还会使可用性探测将完全可用的模型判为"不可路由"， 使其在下拉框中消失一轮。当前实现先嗅探首块（≤4 KB）按形状分流，再将已读取的字节 重新注入流中，实时性不受影响；src/http.js 的 sniffBody 为唯一判据。 ## 为什么速度那一栏会显示 — 早期版本曾为一条实际仅 ~40 tok/s 的车道报告出 2 941 tok/s。问题不在网关——直连 读包的探针显示 64 个帧跨越 5.6 秒，确为增量投递——而在于分子与分母度量的不是同一段 时间：一次调用计费 422 个输出 token，其中 291 个是未流出任何帧的 reasoning token， 它们在第一个可见 token 之前即已生成完毕，而窗口起点正是该 token。以整段 以整段 completion 耗时除以答案文本落地所用秒数，无法反映解码速度。 因此当前实现仅在"能够容纳分子的那段时间"内输出速率：windowTokens() 将未流出的 reasoning token 从分子中剔除，decodeWindow() 拒绝过短以至于无法计时的窗口以及不真实的 高速率，看板与模型表均改为 插件将已收到的思考作为检查点文本，与原始输入一起发起新请求，要求直接输出整理后的回答。 该机制基于检查点重新发起请求，与上游原生 resume 无关，也不会重放已显示的思考内容。恢复段禁用工具调用；已输出 正文或已开始调用工具的截断回合不执行恢复，以避免内容重复或工具重复执行。 为避免重复长思考，恢复提示要求结论优先、最多 800 词；此为提示层面的约束（非硬性 token 限制），模型可能不遵守。恢复属于降级回答，原始请求中的长篇或逐步分析可能被简化。 每个逻辑回合最多两次物理请求：原始请求加一次恢复。默认总时限 900 秒（15 分钟），恢复段最多 300 秒，且受剩余总时长约束；恢复输出上限 8192 tokens，并继续受用户与模型的上限 约束。首段已知的输出 tokens 会从原始预算中扣除，恢复预算不足 512 tokens 时不发起恢复。 检查点最多 **本插件与上述任何上游厂商无隶属或背书关系。** 各厂商名称与商标归其各自所有者所有，仅在说明来源时引用。 ## 安全与隐私 所有状态写入 DSH_HOME/our-free-model/；用量与设置仅落在本机，不上传至任何位置。 聚合车道的 Key 同样不出本机：它只写入插件自己的 0600 `settings.json`，请求只发往你自己配置的那家提供商，插件接口只回显 `hasKey` 与 同样不会启动监听）——该端口的流量消耗的是本机这条免密车道，不应由一个字符串决定是否向整个子网开放。 局域网访问是另开的一扇门，并不放宽上述规则：本机监听仍只绑回环、修改地址仍被拒绝；需要跨机器使用时必须显式启用"局域网访问"，中继绑定可路由地址，且每个请求都需携带局域网 Key——连 /、/health 这类存活探针也一并鉴权（仅本机监听免 Key 应答存活探测），否则一个未鉴权的应答等同于向整个子网宣告"该主机正在代理"。中继仅转发 /v1/models、/v1/chat/completions、/v1/responses、/v1/messages、/v1/messages/count_tokens 五条白名单路径（各自的去 /v1 写法同样放行），不代理任意 loopback 服务；入口处将局域网 Key 换为本机 Key，因此两把 Key 互不通用；携带跳数标记的请求直接拒绝（508），因此端口即使配置为本机监听的同一端口也不会自环。局域网 Key 同样由 crypto 生成、以 timingSafeEqual 比对、存放于同一 0600 文件中，可在面板上单独轮换。 转发 Key 由 crypto 运行时生成、以 timingSafeEqual 比对、存放于 0600 权限文件中。本仓库不含任何硬编码凭据。/ 与 /health 为存活探针，先于 Key 检查应答，但仅回答"是否在线"，获取模型清单仍需 Key。 插件的 HTTP 路由带请求信任围栏（自 v1.1 修复）：插件的 /api/our-free-model 前缀在 webServer 的最长前缀分发下优先于内核 /api，曾绕过内核鉴权。当前每个请求先经由 composition 的 connection 服务准入（与内核 /api 完全同级的 cookie/token 校验）；connection 缺失的 composition 退回结构化围栏——loopback Host、拒绝跨站 sec-fetch-site、Origin/Referer 必须与 Host 同源同端口，Host 缺失或为空也拒绝（fail closed，不回退至 socket 本地地址）。实测结果：异源 Host/Origin 返回 403，无 cookie 的回环请求返回 401。connection 为逐请求获取，因为浏览器半身要到插件加载之后才将其 provide 出来——若在 apply 时以快照方式读取一次，围栏会在整个进程周期内退化为结构化那一层（本轮将该读取改回快照后，picker-test 的 401 断言立即失败）。 公告 HTML 在客户端经严格白名单渲染：scripts/sanitize-test.mjs 使用 XSS 语料（脚本注入、事件属性、javascript:/data: URL、iframe/svg/form、样式注入、畸形标签）验证全部被丢弃；不经过任何 innerHTML sink。公告源的 feedUrl 可被用户指向任意 URL，因此渲染器按不可信输入处理。 应用内升级的完整性链（v1.3.2 加签）：清单 Ed25519 签名验证（公钥 pin 在 src/updater.js，无签名或验签失败的清单直接拒绝，未签名镜像不会被安装）→ 清单校验（semver、路径逃逸、哈希格式、base 必须为清单相对路径）→ 下载时逐文件校验 SHA-256 与字节数 → staging 回读校验 → 安装后回读校验 → 任一步失败即恢复备份；安装前强制重新拉取清单，杜绝陈旧清单。文件与代码边界见已知边界一节。 更新通道与 feedUrl 彻底解耦（v1.3.2）：feedUrl 仅重定向公告 feed，永不再重定向升级清单——此前一个设置项即可将升级源指向任意服务器并配以自配平的哈希，等同于将"修改一个设置值"升级为"在宿主进程中执行任意代码"。公告 override 本身也收紧为仅 https（回环 http 除外，本机镜像与测试仍可用）且不得内嵌凭据。目标域不受限制：任何 https 地址均可作为 feedUrl，插件按 feedPollMinutes 的间隔轮询——因此在不含 connection 服务的 composition 中（见上文鉴权说明），能够修改设置的本机调用者可让进程持续请求任意外部地址。这与插件的其余外联一样按"设置即信任"对待：能够修改 settings.json 的人本来就能安装代码。 转发监听仅绑回环地址，且按解析结果绑定（v1.3.2）：localhost 这类主机名先经 dns.lookup 解析、全部结果均为回环才放行，绑定使用解析出的 IP——当 hosts 文件或企业 DNS 将 localhost 指向可路由接口时，校验与监听不再各自为政。 卸载只需移除 bundle 条目，插件不留任何补丁；其数据目录为纯 JSON，可直接删除。 ## 许可证 MIT，见 LICENSE。 本项目为独立插件，与任何模型提供方无隶属、认可或赞助关系。使用该插件访问免费额度受各提供方 自身条款约束；在超出个人机器的场景中部署前，请先确认这些条款。 ## Star 趋势 图表由 Star History 自动更新，无需手动提交图片。受服务缓存（当前为 24 小时）和 GitHub 图片缓存影响，显示可能延迟，并非秒级实时；点击图表可查看在线趋势。

items.readme_text:
# Hallmark **A design skill for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode that refuses to look AI-generated.** [usehallmark.com](https://www.usehallmark.com)  ·  forty-eight themes  ·  custom on request  ·  redesign and audit by name Made by Together AI.

Hallmark holds a hard floor and then gets out of the way. It deals three themes from a catalog of forty-eight materials, builds the page around what the visitor came to do, and lints the result in a real browser against the tells that read as machine-made: the eyebrow above every heading, tracked-capital labels, one coloured word in a headline, a page of empty frames or nothing but photographs, a hero that misses its screen, an email sign-up at the end of every page, a form that says thanks without sending anything. A fresh-context reviewer gets the last word. The gates come in tiers. The **Floor** never ships (contrast, focus, reduced motion, invented facts, a broken phone layout). **Reflex** gates are the defaults a model falls into; a build with a reason may overrule one on the record. **Finish** checks are craft detail that never blocks a ship. ## New in v2 - **Forty-eight themes.** Each is a material (paper, type, colour, surfaces, its own components and texture) with a picture of a finished page, and the build lays out its own page in it. - **Built from the job.** A booking page books, a shop sells, a newsletter subscribes: the action sits where the category puts it, and the page ends on it. - **Custom.** Ask for a custom page and Hallmark designs from your prompt alone, under the same rules and checks. - **Your real product.** Point it at a URL, a dev server or an app and it captures the screenshots itself. - **Real photographs.** 755 openly licensed photos, picked per subject and credited on the page. - **Redesign and audit.** `/hallmark redesign ` rebuilds a page and keeps its content and wiring; `/hallmark audit ` only reports. ## Themes
Dusk
Closewise, bank reconciliation		 Cobalt
Relay, a webhook API		 Studio
Field Office, an identity studio		 Atelier
Maison Orla, a fragrance atelier		 Ribbon
Lull, a sleep sounds app
Furrow
Fieldbook, farm records		 Dose
Tandem, a family medication app		 Hum
Sprout, a reading game for kids		 Terminal
burrow, a dotfiles CLI		 Hedgerow
Five Mile Gin, a distillery
Ten of the forty-eight. A theme is a material, not a plan: it never says what a page contains or in what order, so two prompts in one theme make two different pages. Each is one file of at most 8 KB in [`references/themes/`](skills/hallmark/references/themes/) with a picture beside it; a build reads exactly one. See them all at [usehallmark.com](https://www.usehallmark.com). ## Custom Say **custom** and Hallmark drops the themes: no plan, no components, no palette recipe, only the floor, the gates and a short direction in [`direction.md`](skills/hallmark/references/direction.md) to find one idea that only this client has and let it run the page. ## How a build runs 1. Pre-flight reads the project (fonts, palette, framework, a locked `design.md`) and asks once for the material: photos, screenshots, real numbers. Nothing is invented. 2. `scripts/theme.mjs deal` offers three themes that fit the prompt and clear the log; `draw` deals the page's anatomy from its job. 3. The hero is built alone, rendered and reviewed cold before the rest of the page exists. 4. `scripts/sloplint.mjs --render` checks the page at eight widths, then a subagent reviews it with fresh eyes. Each page is self-contained HTML and CSS, stamped in its first CSS comment with the decisions it took. ## Redesign Hallmark never starts on a design that already exists unless you name it: ``` /hallmark redesign ./src/app /hallmark audit ./index.html ``` A full redesign keeps the content and the wiring and changes the system and the layout; say *keep the layout* for a restyle or *polish* for only the tells. `sloplint --before` records every link, field, handler and heading first, `sloplint --kept` fails the redesign if one went missing, and the handoff is a side-by-side before and after. ## Install ``` npx skills add nutlope/hallmark -g ``` `-g` installs for every project; leave it off to install into the current one. Needs Node 18 or later. The browser checks (`sloplint --render`, screenshots) also need `npm i -g puppeteer-core` and Chrome; without them the static checks still run. | Harness | Lands in | Invoke | | --- | --- | --- | | Claude Code | `~/.claude/skills/hallmark` | `/hallmark ` or describe a new build | | Codex CLI | `~/.agents/skills/hallmark` | `$hallmark ` or describe a new build | | Cursor | finds the copies above | `/hallmark ` or describe a new build | | OpenCode | finds the copies above | `/hallmark ` or describe a new build | - **One harness only:** `npx skills add nutlope/hallmark -g --agent claude-code` (or `codex`, `opencode`, `cursor`, `github-copilot`). - **As a Claude Code plugin:** `/plugin marketplace add nutlope/hallmark`, then `/plugin install hallmark@hallmark` (invoked as `/hallmark:hallmark`). - **From a clone:** `node skills/hallmark/scripts/install.mjs` validates every theme and reference before it copies; `install-hook.mjs` adds an edit-time Floor check to Claude Code. - **Lint any page:** `node skills/hallmark/scripts/sloplint.mjs --render`. - **If it does not fire on its own,** name it: *use hallmark to build ...*. ## Licence MIT. Use it, fork it, ship it. The photo library (`skills/hallmark/scripts/photos.json`) lists photographs hosted on Wikimedia Commons and holds no image files. Each keeps its own licence (CC0, public domain, CC BY or CC BY-SA), and Hallmark credits every one it uses on the page. It does not use stock sites (Unsplash, Pexels, Pixabay), whose terms bar AI tools from picking their images.
